questions.title: Comprehensions practice 1
questions.explanation: The expression `n + 1` runs once for each input value. Adding one to 2, 4, and 6 produces 3, 5, and 7.

questions.title: Comprehensions practice 2
questions.prompt: Which expression creates a dictionary that maps each word to its length?
choices: {word: len(word) for word in words}
[word, len(word) for word in words]
{len(word) for word in words}
dict(word for len(word) in words)
questions.explanation: A dictionary comprehension needs a key expression, a colon, and a value expression before the for clause. Here each word is the key and its length is the value.

questions.title: Trace Comprehensions
questions.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]
squares = [number * number for number in numbers]
print(squares)
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: Read the comprehension as: make `number * number` for each number in the range. It creates a new list and does not change the range. The resulting output is '[1, 4, 9, 16]'.

questions.title: Comprehensions practice 5
questions.code:
even_squares = [n * n for n in numbers
                if n % 2 == 0]
questions.prompt: What does `[n * n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]` produce for `numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]`?
questions.explanation: The `if` keeps only even numbers (2 and 4), and the `n * n` squares each survivor, giving [4, 16]. [1, 4, 9, 16] would be every square with no filter; [2, 4] is the evens unsquared; [1, 9] is the odds squared. The filter runs first, then the expression.

questions.title: When a loop is clearer
questions.prompt: When should a normal loop replace a comprehension?
choices: When the rule needs several steps, logging, or error handling.
Whenever the result is a new list.
Only when the input collection is empty.
Whenever the expression uses a variable name.
questions.explanation: Comprehensions are best for compact transformations and filters. If the code needs several temporary values, multiple branches, logging, or exception handling, a normal loop is easier to read and debug. Clarity wins over squeezing everything onto one line.

questions.title: Creating a new collection
questions.prompt: What job does a list comprehension usually do?
choices: Mutate the original list one item at a time.
Build a new list from an expression and optional filter.
Print each item without keeping any result.
Catch exceptions from every loop automatically.
questions.explanation: A list comprehension returns a new list. It does not edit the old list unless the expression itself mutates objects, which is usually a smell. If the goal is side effects such as printing or saving files, a plain loop communicates that better.

questions.title: Simple expression and filter
questions.prompt: A comprehension has an expression, a loop, and an optional filter. What keeps it readable?
choices: Use nested conditions even when the line becomes hard to scan.
Hide several assignments inside the expression.
Keep the transformation and filter short enough to understand at a glance.
Use a comprehension even when there is no result to collect.
questions.explanation: Readers should be able to see what each input item becomes and which items are kept. Once the expression or filter needs a lot of explanation, a normal loop gives those steps room. A readable comprehension should feel like a compact sentence, not a puzzle.

questions.title: Avoid side effects
questions.prompt: Why is `[print(name) for name in names]` usually a poor use of a comprehension?
choices: Printing is impossible inside Python loops.
It changes `names` into a tuple.
It always prints in reverse order.
It creates a throwaway list just to cause a side effect.
questions.explanation: The point of a list comprehension is the list it returns. If the returned list is ignored and the only goal is printing, a normal `for` loop is clearer and avoids building a useless list of return values from `print`.

questions.title: Choosing brackets
questions.prompt: Which comprehension shape creates a dictionary from words to lengths?
choices: `{word: len(word) for word in words}`
`[word: len(word) for word in words]`
`(word, len(word) for word in words)`
`{len(word) for word in words: word}`
questions.explanation: A dictionary comprehension uses braces with `key: value` before the loop. A list comprehension uses brackets and one expression, while a set comprehension uses braces with one expression. The colon is the clue that the result maps keys to values.

questions.title: Readability limit
questions.prompt: A comprehension is so packed that classmates keep misreading it. What is the best next step?
choices: Add more conditions so the pattern is fully compressed.
Rewrite it as a normal loop with named intermediate steps.
Remove spaces to make the line shorter.
Keep it because shorter code is always better.
questions.explanation: Comprehensions are not a contest to make the shortest line. A normal loop can name intermediate values and split decisions across lines, which helps readers and debuggers. Use the form that makes the rule easiest to trust.
